# Enrollment is declining

**Cambridge has fewer students than it used to — 152 fewer K-12 students in 2025–26 than in 2015–16, a decline of roughly 18%.**

Fewer students mean:

-

[CLAUDE: This bullet is empty and will show on the page as a blank bullet. Fill it or cut the list.]



 This matters because fewer students mean less state aid, a smaller tax base to spread costs across, and tough choices about staffing and programs. [CLAUDE: Two of these three are not what the data show. (1) State aid: Cambridge's Foundation Aid rose every year, from $7.47 million in 2015–16 to $9.55 million in 2025–26. That is up 28% while enrollment fell 18%. After inflation it is down about 7% in total and up about 13% per pupil. (2) Tax base: enrollment does not set the tax base. Cambridge's taxable full value rose from $504 million to $813 million over these years. What shrinks is the number of students the same costs are spread over.] Enrollment is the starting point for everything that follows: staffing levels, spending per pupil, and the district's fiscal health.

The figure below shows how Cambridge's K-12 enrollment has changed since 2015–16, alongside nearby districts for context.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import os
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.getcwd())

import polars as pl
from plotnine import (
    aes,
    geom_hline,
    geom_line,
    geom_point,
    ggplot,
    labs,
    scale_color_manual,
    scale_x_continuous,
    scale_y_continuous,
)
from great_tables import GT, loc, md, style

import comparisons as cc

# Years shown: ten school years apart.
FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR = 2016, 2026
def _school_year(year_end: int) -> str:
    """2026 -> '2025–26'."""
    return f"{year_end - 1}–{str(year_end)[2:]}"


SPAN = f"{_school_year(FIRST_YEAR)} to {_school_year(LAST_YEAR)}"

enr = (
    cc.panel_for(cc.GRAPH_GROUP, since=FIRST_YEAR)
    .filter(pl.col("year_end") <= LAST_YEAR)
    .select("district", "region", "year_end", "k12_enrollment")
    .drop_nulls()
)

# --- Checks: the numbers written out in the prose must match the data. --------
assert (enr["year_end"].min(), enr["year_end"].max()) == (FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR)
assert enr.group_by("district").len()["len"].unique().to_list() == [LAST_YEAR - FIRST_YEAR + 1]


def _n(district: str, year_end: int) -> int:
    return int(
        enr.filter((pl.col("district") == district) & (pl.col("year_end") == year_end))[
            "k12_enrollment"
        ].item()
    )


_chg = {d: _n(d, LAST_YEAR) - _n(d, FIRST_YEAR) for d in cc.GRAPH_GROUP.values()}
_pct = {d: round(_chg[d] / _n(d, FIRST_YEAR) * 100) for d in _chg}
assert (_chg["Cambridge"], _pct["Cambridge"]) == (-152, -18)
assert (_chg["Schuylerville"], _pct["Schuylerville"]) == (-359, -22)
assert (_chg["Greenwich"], _pct["Greenwich"]) == (-232, -22)
assert _chg["Salem"] > -10 and _chg["Hoosick Falls"] > -60  # "closer to flat"
# Cambridge's decline is third-largest of the five, by count and by percent.
assert sorted(_chg, key=_chg.get).index("Cambridge") == 2
_exact = {d: _chg[d] / _n(d, FIRST_YEAR) for d in _chg}
assert sorted(_exact, key=_exact.get).index("Cambridge") == 2
assert (_n("Schuylerville", FIRST_YEAR), _n("Salem", FIRST_YEAR)) == (1645, 512)
# 2020-21: four of the five lost students (Salem did not); only Cambridge had
# more students the next year; none of the four later regained its 2019-20 level.
_lost = [d for d in _chg if _n(d, 2021) < _n(d, 2020)]
assert sorted(_lost) == ["Cambridge", "Greenwich", "Hoosick Falls", "Schuylerville"]
assert [d for d in _lost if _n(d, 2022) > _n(d, 2021)] == ["Cambridge"]
assert all(
    max(_n(d, y) for y in range(2021, LAST_YEAR + 1)) < _n(d, 2020) for d in _lost
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-enrollment
#| fig-cap: "K–12 enrollment by school year ending, 2016 (2015–16) through 2026 (2025–26). Source: NYSED BEDS Day enrollment (first Wednesday of October)."
g = enr.select("district", "year_end", "k12_enrollment")
cambridge = g.filter(pl.col("district") == cc.FOCUS)

(
    ggplot(g, aes("year_end", "k12_enrollment", color="district"))
    + geom_line(size=1)
    + geom_point(size=1.8)
    + geom_line(cambridge, size=2.4)  # emphasize the focus district
    + scale_color_manual(
        values=cc.PALETTE, name="", limits=cc.district_order(cc.GRAPH_GROUP)
    )
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=list(range(FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR + 1)))
    + scale_y_continuous(limits=(450, 1400), breaks=list(range(500, 1401, 200)))
    + labs(
        x="School year ending",
        y="K–12 enrollment",
        title=f"K-12 enrollment, {SPAN}",
    )
    + cc.theme_ccs()
)
```

The districts differ greatly in size, which is why the chart above clips Schuylerville (1,645 students in 2016) off the top while bunching Salem (512) near the bottom. Setting each district's 2016 enrollment equal to 100 puts them on one shared scale, so the lines compare **rates** of change rather than size:

```{python}
#| label: fig-enrollment-indexed
#| fig-cap: "K–12 enrollment indexed to 2016 (= 100); 90 means a 10% decline. Dashed line marks the 2016 baseline. Source: NYSED BEDS Day enrollment."
g = enr.select("district", "year_end", "k12_enrollment")
# set each district's 2016 enrollment equal to 100
base = (
    g.filter(pl.col("year_end") == FIRST_YEAR)
    .select("district", "k12_enrollment")
    .rename({"k12_enrollment": "base_2016"})
)
idx = g.join(base, on="district").with_columns(
    (pl.col("k12_enrollment") / pl.col("base_2016") * 100).alias("index")
)
cambridge = idx.filter(pl.col("district") == cc.FOCUS)

(
    ggplot(idx, aes("year_end", "index", color="district"))
    + geom_hline(yintercept=100, linetype="dashed", color="#999999")
    + geom_line(size=1)
    + geom_point(size=1.8)
    + geom_line(cambridge, size=2.4)  # emphasize the focus district
    + scale_color_manual(
        values=cc.PALETTE, name="", limits=cc.district_order(cc.GRAPH_GROUP)
    )
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=list(range(FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR + 1)))
    + scale_y_continuous(limits=(75, 110), breaks=list(range(75, 111, 5)))
    + labs(
        x="School year ending",
        y="K–12 enrollment, indexed (2016 = 100)",
        title="K-12 enrollment indexed to 2016 (= 100)",
    )
    + cc.theme_ccs()
)
```

Cambridge's enrollment decline is real, but it is not alone. **The trend is regional.** Schuylerville and Greenwich have seen larger absolute losses (359 and 232 students respectively), while Hoosick Falls and Salem have held steadier. The table below shows where each district stood in 2015–16 and 2025–26, and how much they gained or lost over the decade.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-enrollment-change
#| tbl-cap: "K–12 enrollment in 2015–16 and 2025–26, with change, by district."
g = enr.filter(pl.col("year_end").is_in([FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR]))

wide = (
    g.with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col("region") == "Washington County").then(0).otherwise(1).alias("_rank")
    )
    .pivot(values="k12_enrollment", index=["_rank", "region", "district"], on="year_end")
    .sort(["_rank", "district"])
    .drop("_rank")
)

wide = wide.with_columns(
    (pl.col("2026") - pl.col("2016")).alias("change"),
    ((pl.col("2026") - pl.col("2016")) / pl.col("2016") * 100).alias("pct_change"),
)

(
    GT(wide, rowname_col="district", groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(
        title="K-12 enrollment change",
        subtitle="School-year-ending 2016 (2015–16) and 2026 (2025–26), with change"
    )
    .fmt_number(columns=["2016", "2026", "change"], decimals=0)
    .fmt_number(columns="pct_change", decimals=1, force_sign=True)
    .tab_spanner(label="School year ending", columns=["2016", "2026"])
    .cols_label(pct_change=md("% change"))
    .tab_style(
        style=[style.fill(color="#FCEFB4"), style.text(weight="bold")],
        locations=[
            loc.body(rows=pl.col("district") == cc.FOCUS),
            loc.stub(rows=pl.col("district") == cc.FOCUS),
        ],
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        md(
            "**Source:** NYSED BEDS Day enrollment database. K-12 enrollment as of "
            "the first Wednesday of October."
        )
    )
)
```

**Cambridge lost 152 students (−18%)** over the decade, the third-largest decline among the five districts, whether counted in students or in percent. Schuylerville lost 359 students (−22%) and Greenwich lost 232 (−22%). Salem and Hoosick Falls held closer to flat.

## What this means

Enrollment decline sets the context for everything else in Cambridge's budget:

- **State aid is tied to students.** Fewer students mean less foundation aid from New York State, unless the state adjusts its formulas. [CLAUDE: Not what happened in Cambridge; see my note near the top. A sentence the data support: "State aid has not fallen as enrollment fell, but it has not kept up with inflation."]
- **Fixed costs don't shrink.** A building, a bus route, a principal — these costs don't automatically fall when enrollment does. Spreading fixed costs over fewer students is part of why Cambridge's **spending per pupil** ranks high (see the [Spending](spending.qmd) chapter).
- **Staffing choices get harder.** Cambridge now has the **fewest students per teacher** of the comparison group (see the [Students per teacher](students-per-teacher.qmd) chapter) — a choice that preserves small classes but adds pressure at budget time. [CLAUDE: Three problems. "Fewest of the comparison group" is true of the five (8.7 in 2024–25) but not of the twelve: Fort Edward, Hartford and Whitehall are lower. "A choice" states a motive the data do not show. And "small classes" treats students per teacher as class size, which it is not. I would write: "Cambridge has the fewest students per teacher of the five districts shown here."]

The enrollment trend is a regional challenge, not unique to Cambridge. But the scale of the decline — and the decisions it forces about what to preserve — is what Cambridge's community must grapple with.
